idiom_name: interface contract + class with private readonly parameter properties, wired by a container
implementation_notes: The classic structure maps directly onto TypeScript: declare the operation on an interface, implement it in a class whose constructor takes collaborators as private readonly parameter properties, and let a container (NestJS providers/@Injectable, tsyringe, or a hand-written composition root) supply them. The framework-free alternative is a module of functions taking a deps object, so keep the class form when a container already owns lifetimes or when several operations share one dependency set. Because interfaces are erased at run time, containers need a class or a Symbol as the injection token - abstract classes are the usual compromise.
pitfalls: private readonly is compile-time only: nothing stops a method from assigning to a mutable field or closing over request state, so statelessness remains a review-and-test discipline.
Interfaces vanish at run time, so an interface used as a DI token silently resolves to the wrong provider (or throws) unless an abstract class or matching Symbol is used.
Injecting a request-scoped provider into a singleton-scoped service captures one request's state - the classic NestJS scoping trap.

variants.name: Stateless module functions (fn(args, deps))
variants.idiom_name: exported domain function whose second parameter is an explicit deps object
variants.implementation_notes: Replace the injected class with a plain function whose second parameter carries the collaborators (convert(amount, target, deps)), typed as an inline structural type or a Deps type; the composition root binds real adapters and tests pass fakes. Because the dependency list lives in the signature instead of a constructor, a service that keeps needing more repositories is visible in review, and no container or decorator metadata is required - this is the framework-free form to prefer in a hexagonal codebase. Choose the class form when lifetimes are container-managed or when one dependency set must be shared by many operations.
pitfalls: Every call site must thread deps through; one forgotten layer pushes the wiring (importing a concrete adapter) into domain code.

A module of functions has no lifecycle, so scoped resources - a transaction, a request-bound session - cannot be captured by the service and must be passed explicitly or owned by the application layer.
Nothing prevents a deps type from naming infrastructure types (a SQL client); keep the structural type expressed in domain terms to preserve the dependency direction.
